metadata.note: Yes -- Sarnia, Ontario had a through rail connection to Detroit, and its opening date is a remarkable coincidence: Nov 21 1859, when BOTH halves opened simultaneously. On the Canadian side, the Grand Trunk Railway completed its Toronto-Sarnia line, reaching Point Edward (just north of Sarnia) that day -- part of the original Grand Trunk Railway of Canada main line (Toronto Union Station opened 1858; the Montreal-Toronto trunk itself completed the following year). On the American side, the Chicago, Detroit & Canada Grand Trunk Junction Railroad (chartered Mar 16 1858 specifically to link Detroit-Port Huron, 60 miles) opened that same day, running via Mount Clemens. A ferry carried railcars and passengers across the St. Clair River between Point Edward and Fort Gratiot/Port Huron from the start -- loading and unloading was slow and the crossing was plagued by current, ice, and Great Lakes shipping traffic. The Grand Trunk organized the St. Clair Tunnel Company in 1886 to fix this, and the St. Clair Tunnel opened Sept 19 1891: the first underwater railway tunnel in North America and the world's first international rail tunnel (6,025ft, with approaches totaling 11,553ft). Coke-fired steam locomotives hauled trains through at first; after a fatal fume accident killed six men Oct 10 1904, electric locomotives took over in 1908. The corridor's flagship was the International Limited, an overnight Grand Trunk/Canadian National (Canada nationalized Grand Trunk in 1923)/Grand Trunk Western train running as far as Montreal; it was cut back to Port Huron in 1970 and discontinued entirely in 1971, just before Amtrak's May 1 1971 creation. Amtrak and VIA Rail revived the corridor Oct 31 1982 (extending Amtrak's Blue Water Limited from Port Huron to Toronto, renamed the International in 1983) -- but that joint service was itself discontinued April 2004, killed by post-9/11 border-crossing delays, the 2003 SARS outbreak, and falling ridership (down from 125,126 riders in 1997 to 88,045 in 2003). Today VIA Rail still runs Toronto-Sarnia and Amtrak still runs Chicago-Port Huron (as the Blue Water), but the two no longer connect as a through train -- there is no cross-border passenger rail at Sarnia/Port Huron today. Geometry is a real-town waypoint approximation (Sarnia/Point Edward-Port Huron-Mount Clemens-Detroit), straight-line segments between documented stations -- NOT digitized from period track maps.
